questions.q: Ask the user for a word. Take off any spaces at each end of it. Display nothing typed when nothing is left. Otherwise display value [the word without those spaces].

teach.say: .strip() takes the spaces off each end of what was typed, so a line of nothing but spaces becomes the empty string and can be caught.
code: entry = input().strip()   # the user typed three spaces

brief: One line only is printed.
A line of nothing but spaces is not a word.
Print exactly: nothing typed

tests.why: An ordinary word should be accepted and printed back after the word value.
Pressing enter with nothing typed is the empty string, and that is the case a presence check exists for.
Five spaces look like nothing on screen but are not the empty string - strip them before you test for empty.
The word is real but padded. Strip it once and use the stripped version, or the stray spaces end up in your output.

questions.fb: A presence check means checking the input is not empty once the spaces around it have been removed.

questions.q: Ask the user for a whole number. Check whether every character typed is a digit. Display number: [the number] when they are all digits. Display not a number instead when any one of them is not.
brief: A minus sign is not a digit.
A decimal point is not a digit.
An empty line is not a number.
One line only is printed.

tests.why: Digits only, so this is a whole number and the number itself is printed after the label.
Letters are not digits. Calling int() on this straight away would crash the program, which is what a type check prevents.
Nothing typed at all is not a whole number either - isdigit() is False for the empty string.
A decimal point is not a digit, so this fails the check even though it is a number.
The brief says digits only, and a minus sign is not a digit - so this one is refused here on purpose.
Zero is a perfectly good whole number. A check that tests whether the number is true rather than whether it is digits would reject it.

questions.fb: isdigit() asks the question safely, before int() gets the chance to crash.

questions.q: Ask the user for a word. Check it against red, green and blue, which are fixed in the program. Display known when it is one of those three. Display unknown instead when it is not.
brief: The three allowed words are written into the program, not typed in.
Matching is exact, so a capital letter makes a word unknown.
One line only is printed.

tests.why: The first of the three allowed words. A check that only looks at one of them passes here and fails the next test.
Every one of the three has to be allowed, so all three belong in the condition.
The last of the three. If this came out unknown, your or is missing its third comparison.
A word that is not on the list at all must be refused, whatever else it looks like.
A capital R makes a different word, because == compares exactly. This is the case a look-up check is usually asked about.
Nothing typed is not one of the three either, so it is unknown rather than a crash.

questions.fb: A look-up check compares what was typed against the values the program already holds, so each allowed value needs its own complete comparison: entry == 'red' or entry == 'green', not entry == 'red' or 'green'.

questions.q: Ask the user for a whole number. Display valid when it is from 1 to 10 inclusive. Display too low instead when it is below 1. Display too high instead when it is above 10.
brief: Both 1 and 10 are allowed.
One line only is printed.

tests.why: An ordinary number comfortably inside the range.
1 is the bottom boundary and inclusive means it is allowed - if you got too low you used < 2 or <= 1 the wrong way round.
10 is the top boundary and is allowed. This is where < and <= get confused.
One below the boundary, so it must be refused. 0 is the value a range check most often lets through by mistake.
One above the boundary. Testing > 10 rather than >= 10 is what makes this one work.
Well below the range, and still too low rather than too high.

questions.fb: Inclusive means both boundaries pass, so the four values worth testing are 0, 1, 10 and 11.

questions.q: Ask the user for a whole number. Display not a number when what was typed is not a whole number. Display ok when it is from -5 to 35 inclusive. Display out of range when it is outside that range.
brief: A minus sign at the front is allowed.
A decimal point is not allowed.
Both -5 and 35 are allowed.
One line only is printed.
questions.starter: # a negative number is still a number

tests.why: An ordinary value inside the range.
The bottom boundary is negative, so isdigit() on its own cannot accept it - this is where try and except earn their place.
One step below the boundary. With negatives it is easy to write the comparison the wrong way round.
The top boundary is inclusive and must be accepted.
One above the top boundary, so out of range.
A word cannot be turned into a number, so int() raises an error that must be caught instead of crashing.
int() refuses a decimal point too, so this is reported as not a number rather than rounded.

questions.fb: try and except around int() catch the wrong type; the range test then runs only on a value you know is a number.

questions.q: Ask the user for a word. Display too short when it is under 8 characters. Display too long when it is over 16 characters. Display ok for anything in between.
brief: Count the line exactly as it is typed, with no stripping.
An empty line is too short.
One line only is printed.

tests.why: Ten characters is inside the range, so this one passes.
Seven characters is one short of the minimum, so it must be refused.
Exactly 8 characters is allowed - if this prints too short you used <= 8 instead of < 8.
Exactly 16 characters is the top boundary and is still allowed.
Seventeen characters is one over the maximum, which is the boundary a length check usually misses.
Nothing typed has length 0, which is fewer than 8 - so too short, not a crash.

questions.fb: len() gives the length; the two boundaries worth testing are 7 and 8 at one end, 16 and 17 at the other.

questions.q: Ask the user for a code. Take off any spaces at each end of it. Display valid code when it is two letters and then four digits. Display invalid code instead when it is not.
brief: It must be exactly 6 characters.
Capitals and small letters both count as letters.
One line only is printed.

tests.why: Two letters then four digits, so this is the shape the check is looking for.
Small letters are allowed, so isalpha() is the right test rather than comparing against the capitals.
Only five characters. Check the length first, or slicing a short string quietly gives you a shorter piece and the check passes.
Seven characters. A check that only looks at the first six characters would let this through.
The second character is a digit, not a letter, so the letters part fails.
The third character is a letter, so the four digits are not all digits.
Nothing typed must be refused rather than crash - the length test catches it before any slicing matters.

questions.fb: A format check is a length check and a check on what each part contains, and both have to pass.

questions.q: Keep asking the user for a word until one still has something in it once the spaces at each end have been taken off. Display that is empty for every wrong one. Then display accepted [the word without those spaces] for the one you take.
brief: Print nothing else.
Read no more lines once one is accepted.
Print exactly: that is empty
questions.starter: # keep going until something is really typed

tests.why: A word first time needs no message at all - do not print the warning before you have checked.
One empty line, one message, then the word is accepted. A loop that only checks once would accept the empty line.
Spaces and then nothing are both empty, and the accepted word is printed without its padding.
It has to keep asking however many times it takes, so the message appears once for each empty line.

questions.fb: The usual shape is to read once, then a while loop that prints the message and reads again while the value is still wrong.

questions.q: Keep asking the user for a whole number until one is from 1 to 5 inclusive. Display please enter 1 to 5 for every wrong one. Then display chosen [the number] for the one you accept.
brief: Print nothing else.
Read no more lines once one is accepted.
Both 1 and 5 are allowed.
questions.starter: # keep going until it is 1 to 5

tests.why: A valid number first time needs no message at all - do not print the warning before you have checked.
One bad go, one message, then the good one is accepted. A loop that only checks once would accept the 9.
It has to keep asking however many times it takes, and 5 is the top boundary so it is allowed.
1 is the bottom boundary. If this prints a warning, your condition is refusing the value it should accept.
6 is one over the top. Reading the next number inside the loop is what gives the user another go.

questions.fb: The condition on the while is the opposite of the one that accepts, so read once before the loop and again at the bottom of it.

questions.q: Keep asking the user for a whole number until one is from 10 to 99 inclusive. Display that is not a whole number when what was typed is not all digits. Display that is outside 10 to 99 when it is a number outside that range. Then display accepted: [the number] for the one you accept.
brief: Check whether it is all digits before checking the range.
Both 10 and 99 are allowed.
Nothing more is read once one is accepted.

tests.why: Valid straight away, so the only line printed is the acceptance.

out: that is not a whole number
tests.why: A word is the wrong type, so the type message comes first - checking the range before the type would crash here.
Both 9 and 100 are the right type but outside the range, and 10 is the bottom boundary so it is accepted.

out: that is not a whole number
that is not a whole number
tests.why: Nothing typed and a decimal both fail the type check, and 99 is the top boundary so it is accepted.
0 is digits, so it gets the range message and not the type message.

questions.fb: Check the type first and the range second, because a range test on text that is not a number is what crashes the program.

questions.q: Ask the user for a line of usernames. Then ask for a line of passwords in the same order. Then ask for one username to check. Then ask for one password to check. Display unknown user when the username is not listed. Display wrong password when the password does not match. Display access granted when both match.
brief: Both lines are separated by single spaces.
Matching is exact, with capitals counting.
One line only is printed.
questions.starter: # a username and a password to check

tests.why: Both halves match, so access is granted. Make sure you compare against the password in the same position as the username.
A different account must work the same way - a program that only ever checks the first user fails here.
Only the first letter differs in case, and that is still a different password - do not lower() the password before comparing.
A real username with another user's password must be refused, so the two checks have to be tied together.
No such username, so the answer is unknown user even though the password belongs to somebody.
The username is in capitals and the match is exact, so this counts as an unknown user.
A different pair of lists, so accounts written into the program instead of read in will fail here.

questions.fb: Find the username first; only once you know where it is can you look up the password that belongs with it.

questions.q: Ask the user for the correct passcode. Then ask for one attempt at a time. Display wrong passcode for each miss. Display access granted as soon as one matches. Then display account locked if a third attempt has missed too.
brief: Matching is exact, with capitals counting.
No more than three attempts are read.
Nothing is read after a match.

tests.why: Right first time, so nothing else is printed - no warning and certainly no lock.
One wrong go then the right one. The loop must stop as soon as it is right, not use up all three attempts.
Any wrong passcode gets the same message, and the second attempt still works.
The third attempt is still allowed, so this must be granted rather than locked.
Three failures lock the account. If your program asks for a fourth passcode it will run out of input and crash.
A passcode in the wrong case is wrong, so the first attempt fails - passwords are case sensitive.
A different passcode entirely, so one written into the program rather than read in will fail here.

questions.fb: Count the attempts and stop on either condition: three used up, or the right passcode given.

questions.q: Keep asking the user for a username until one is 5 to 12 characters of letters and digits only. Then keep asking for a whole number until one is from 11 to 19 inclusive. Display registered [the username] [the number] at the end.
brief: Reject a username of the wrong length with exactly username must be 5 to 12 characters.
When the length is fine but a character is not a letter or digit, reject it with exactly username must be letters and digits only.
Reject something that is not a whole number with exactly number must be a whole number.
Reject a number outside the range with exactly number must be 11 to 19.
Separate the three parts of the last line with single spaces.
questions.starter: # each rule its own message, checked in order

tests.why: Both valid first time, so the only line printed is the registration.
Four characters is one short, five is the boundary and allowed, and 11 is the bottom of the number range.
Twelve characters is the top boundary for the username and 19 the top of the number range, so both are accepted.
Thirteen characters is one over the top and fin9 is one under the bottom, so both get the length message - the loop has to keep asking after each one.

out: username must be letters and digits only
username must be letters and digits only
tests.why: A space and a hyphen are both long enough but neither is a letter or a digit, so the second rule catches them.

out: number must be a whole number
number must be a whole number
tests.why: Nothing typed and a word both fail the type check; 10 and 20 are one outside each end of the range.

questions.fb: Each rule gets its own message and the checks go in order, so the user is told the one thing that is actually wrong.

questions.q: Keep asking the user for word,number lines until one is exactly done. Display added [the word] for each good line. Then display accepted: [how many were added] on the next line. Then display total: [their numbers added up] on the last line.
brief: Spaces around either field are ignored.
A wrong line must never stop the run.
Check the commas first, and print exactly bad line when there is not exactly one.
Then print exactly bad number when the number is not all digits.
Then print exactly out of range when the number is outside 1 to 99.
questions.starter: # report a bad line and carry on to the next one

tests.why: Two good lines, so both are added and the total is the two numbers added together.
No data at all is not an error - the counters start at 0 and both are printed.
No comma and two commas are both bad lines, and neither may stop the program.
A number in words must be reported rather than passed to int(), which would crash the whole run.
0 and 100 are one outside each boundary; 1 and 99 are the boundaries themselves and are allowed.
The spaces round the word and the number must be stripped, or the word prints padded and the digit check fails.

questions.fb: Defensive design means a wrong line is reported and skipped, not allowed to stop the whole run.
